question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to BENEVOLENT.
explanation_en: Benevolent means well-meaning and kindly.

question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to CANDID.
explanation_en: Candid means truthful and straightforward, i.e. frank.

question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to OBSOLETE.
explanation_en: Obsolete describes something no longer in use or out of date.

question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to METICULOUS.
explanation_en: Meticulous means showing great attention to detail; painstaking is the nearest synonym.

question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to EPHEMERAL.
explanation_en: Ephemeral things last for a very short time.

question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to ABATE.
explanation_en: To abate is to become less intense, e.g. the storm abated; subside is closest.

question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to ARDENT.
explanation_en: Ardent means enthusiastic and passionate.

question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to FRUGAL.
explanation_en: Frugal means careful about spending money, i.e. thrifty.

question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to PERNICIOUS.
explanation_en: Pernicious means having a gradual but destructive, harmful effect.

question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to CAPRICIOUS.
explanation_en: Capricious means given to sudden changes of mood or behaviour, i.e. fickle.

question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to SAGACIOUS.
explanation_en: Sagacious means having sound judgement; wise is its synonym.

question_en: Select the word closest in meaning to TENACIOUS.
explanation_en: Tenacious means holding firmly to a purpose; persistent is nearest.

question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to GENEROUS.
explanation_en: Generous means giving freely; its antonym is stingy (unwilling to give).

question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to SCARCE.
explanation_en: Scarce means in short supply; abundant means plentiful.

question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to EXPAND.
explanation_en: Expand means to become larger; contract means to become smaller.

question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to AMATEUR.
explanation_en: An amateur is non-professional; the opposite is professional.

question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to VERBOSE.
explanation_en: Verbose means using more words than needed; concise means brief and to the point.

question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to TRANSPARENT.
explanation_en: Transparent allows light to pass through; opaque does not.

question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to DILIGENT.
explanation_en: Diligent means hard-working; indolent means habitually lazy.

question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to BENIGN.
explanation_en: Benign means harmless or gentle; malignant means harmful or disease-causing (e.g. a malignant tumour).

question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to INEVITABLE.
explanation_en: Inevitable means unable to be avoided; avoidable is its opposite.

question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to ZENITH.
explanation_en: Zenith is the highest point; nadir is the lowest point.

question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to TACITURN.
explanation_en: Taciturn means habitually silent; talkative is its antonym.

question_en: Select the word opposite in meaning to MAGNANIMOUS.
explanation_en: Magnanimous means generous and forgiving; petty means small-minded and mean.

question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘That which cannot be read’.
explanation_en: Illegible means impossible to read because of poor handwriting or print; illiterate refers to a person who cannot read.

question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘That which cannot be avoided’.
explanation_en: Inevitable means certain to happen and unavoidable.

question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘One who devotes his life to the welfare of others’.
explanation_en: An altruist is selflessly concerned for the well-being of others; an egoist is self-centred.

question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘Government by a small group of people’.
explanation_en: Oligarchy = rule by a few; democracy = by the people; monarchy/autocracy = by one.

question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘The scientific study of birds’.
explanation_en: Ornithology is the study of birds; entomology is of insects, etymology of word origins.

question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘One who knows everything’.
explanation_en: Omniscient = all-knowing; omnipotent = all-powerful; omnipresent = present everywhere.

question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘A place where bees are kept’.
explanation_en: An apiary houses bees; an aviary houses birds.

question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘The killing of a king’.
explanation_en: Regicide (Latin rex = king) is the killing of a king; fratricide is killing of a brother.

question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘An abnormal fear of open or crowded places’.
explanation_en: Agoraphobia is fear of open spaces; claustrophobia is fear of closed spaces.

question_en: Select the one word that can replace: ‘A person who hates mankind’.
explanation_en: A misanthrope hates or distrusts people in general; a misogynist hates women.

question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘To break the ice’.

options.en: To start a conversation in a social setting

explanation_en: “Break the ice” means to ease the initial awkwardness between people who have just met.

question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘Once in a blue moon’.
explanation_en: “Once in a blue moon” means something that happens extremely rarely.

question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘A piece of cake’.
explanation_en: The idiom describes a task that is very easy to do.

question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘To bite the bullet’.

options.en: To face a painful situation with courage

explanation_en: The phrase means to endure a painful or unpleasant situation bravely.

question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘To burn the midnight oil’.

options.en: To work late into the night

explanation_en: The idiom refers to studying or working until late at night.

question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘Under the weather’.
explanation_en: “Under the weather” means slightly ill or in low spirits.

question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘To beat around the bush’.

options.en: To avoid coming to the main point

explanation_en: The idiom means to talk about unimportant things instead of getting to the point.

question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘A blessing in disguise’.

options.en: Something good that seemed bad at first

explanation_en: It describes a misfortune that eventually turns out to be beneficial.

question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘To cry over spilt milk’.

options.en: To regret something that cannot be undone

explanation_en: The idiom warns against useless grief over past mistakes that cannot be corrected.

question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘Achilles’ heel’.
explanation_en: From Greek myth, Achilles was vulnerable only at his heel; the idiom means a fatal weakness in an otherwise strong person.

question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘Swan song’.

options.en: A final performance or act before retirement

explanation_en: A swan song is the last work or appearance of a person before retirement or death.

question_en: Select the meaning of the idiom: ‘The elephant in the room’.

options.en: An obvious problem that people avoid discussing

explanation_en: The idiom refers to a major issue everyone knows about but nobody wants to talk about.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
The ______ shop sells pens and paper, but the bus outside remained ______ for an hour.
explanation_en: 'Stationery' (with e, as in envelope/pen) means writing materials; 'stationary' (with a) means not moving. So 'stationery shop' and 'remained stationary'.

question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
The ______ of the school praised the student for his high moral ______.
explanation_en: 'Principal' is the head of a school; 'principles' are moral rules or beliefs. So 'The principal ... high moral principles'.

question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The meeting was ______ because the chairman was ill.
explanation_en: 'Call off' means to cancel. 'Call on' means to visit, 'call up' to telephone or summon for military service, and 'call for' to demand or require.

question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Riya takes ______ her mother; both have the same smile and the same patience.
explanation_en: 'Take after' means to resemble an older family member. 'Take up' means to start a hobby, 'take over' to gain control and 'take in' to deceive or absorb.

question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
There was ______ rain throughout the night, and the roads were flooded by morning.
explanation_en: The fixed collocation is 'heavy rain' (also heavy traffic, heavy smoker). 'Strong' goes with wind or tea, and 'thick' with fog.

question_en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The Education Minister ______ a speech at the national conference on teacher training.
explanation_en: We 'deliver' (or give/make) a speech. 'Told' needs a person or a story, 'said' needs the words spoken, and 'spoke' takes 'on' or 'to', not a direct object 'a speech'.

question_en:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given proverb.
Too many cooks spoil the broth.

options.en: Expensive food is often badly made
When too many people handle a task, the result is poor
Many hands make the work light

explanation_en: The proverb warns that when too many people try to manage the same work, they get in each other's way and spoil it. 'Many hands make light work' is a different proverb with the opposite idea.

question_en:
Select the word that can fill both blanks.
The ______ of the river was flooded after the storm. / She deposited her salary in the ______.
explanation_en: 'Bank' is a homonym: the side of a river and a financial institution. 'Shore' fits only the first blank and 'account' only the second.

question_en: Select the sentence with no spelling error.

options.en: The committee will recommend a seperate budget for the library.
The comittee will recommend a separate budget for the library.
The committee will recommend a separate budget for the library.
The committee will reccommend a separate budget for the library.

explanation_en: Correct spellings: committee (double m, double t, double e), recommend (one c, double m) and separate (sep-a-rate). Only option 3 has all three right.

question_en:
Passage: Sleep is often treated as a luxury by students and working adults, yet scientists consider it as essential as food and water. During sleep the brain does not simply switch off; it sorts the information gathered during the day, stores important memories and clears away harmful chemicals that accumulate while we are awake. Children who sleep for less than eight hours are more likely to have difficulty in concentrating and to show poor results in examinations. Adults who regularly sleep for only five or six hours face a higher risk of heart disease and depression. Experts therefore advise a fixed bedtime, avoiding screens an hour before sleeping and keeping the bedroom dark and quiet. Contrary to popular belief, sleeping late on weekends cannot fully repay the “sleep debt” collected during the week.

What is the main idea of the passage?

options.en: Weekends are meant for rest only.
Sleep is essential for health and learning.

explanation_en: The passage opens by calling sleep as essential as food and water, then describes its effects on the brain, children and adults.

Passage: Trees in cities do much more than make streets look pleasant. A single mature tree can absorb about twenty kilograms of carbon dioxide in a year and release enough oxygen for two people. Their leaves trap dust, while their shade can lower the temperature of a neighbourhood by several degrees, reducing the need for air conditioners. In many Indian cities, however, trees are felled for widening roads and constructing flyovers, often without any plan to replace them. Urban planners argue that development and greenery are not enemies; roads can be designed around existing trees, and every felled tree can be compensated by planting several saplings. Citizens, too, must take the initiative by protecting trees in their own colony instead of waiting for the government to act.

What is the central theme of the passage?

options.en: Roads are more important than trees.
Urban trees are valuable and should be protected.

explanation_en: The passage details the benefits of city trees and urges planners and citizens to protect them.

question_en:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
P. Within a few years, the small shop had grown into the largest bookstore in the town.
Q. Ramesh opened a tiny bookshop near the bus stand in 1998 with borrowed money.
R. At first very few customers came, and he often sat alone among the shelves.
S. Slowly, students began to visit because he let them read books free of cost in the shop.
explanation_en: Q introduces Ramesh and the shop, R describes the slow start ('At first'), S the change ('Slowly, students began to visit') and P the result 'within a few years'. Hence QRSP.

question_en:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. Plastic bags take hundreds of years to break down.
B. As a result, they choke drains, harm animals and pollute the soil.
C. Many states have therefore banned single-use plastic bags.
D. Yet millions of them are thrown away every day after a single use.
explanation_en: A states the fact, D adds the contrast with 'Yet' (they are still thrown away daily), B gives the result of that ('As a result, they choke drains'), and C the remedy ('therefore banned'). Hence ADBC.

question_en:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
1) It was then that he decided to become a doctor and serve the poor.
2) When Arun was ten, his grandfather fell seriously ill in their village.
3) The nearest hospital was forty kilometres away, and the old man died on the way.
4) Today he runs a free clinic in the same village.
explanation_en: 2 sets the scene (grandfather's illness), 3 tells what happened, 1 gives the decision ('It was then') which needs 3 before it, and 4 ends in the present ('Today'). Hence 2, 3, 1, 4.

question_en:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
P. In the Middle Ages books were copied by hand, so only the rich could own them.
Q. The invention of the printing press in the fifteenth century changed this.
R. As a result, knowledge, once the property of a few, reached ordinary people.
S. Books could now be produced quickly and sold cheaply.
explanation_en: P gives the old situation, Q the change ('changed this' refers back to P), S the immediate effect of printing ('could now be produced quickly') and R the wider result ('As a result'). Hence PQSR.

question_en:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in the correct order.
The government has decided
P. so that no child
Q. in remote villages
R. is left without education
S. to open new schools
explanation_en: 'Decided' is followed by the infinitive S 'to open new schools', then Q 'in remote villages', then the purpose clause P 'so that no child' and R 'is left without education'. Hence SQPR.

question_en:
Passage: Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi were once the staple food of most Indian households. They grow on poor soil, need very little water and can survive high temperatures, which makes them ideal for a country where more than half the farmland depends on rain. Nutritionally, they are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and they release sugar into the blood slowly, which helps in controlling diabetes. After the Green Revolution of the 1960s, however, government support went mainly to rice and wheat, and millets came to be seen as the 'poor man's food'. Their share in the Indian plate shrank steadily. In recent years the trend has begun to reverse. The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets on India's proposal, and many states now serve millet dishes in school meals. Nutrition experts welcome the change but warn that the revival will last only if farmers receive a fair price for what they grow.

What is the main idea of the passage?

options.en: Rice and wheat are more nutritious than millets.
Millets declined after the Green Revolution and are now being revived.
The Green Revolution was a complete failure.
Millets can be grown only in rain-fed areas.

explanation_en: The passage traces millets from staple food, to decline after the Green Revolution, to the recent revival (International Year of Millets, school meals). The other options are either not stated or contradicted.

question_en:
Passage: Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi were once the staple food of most Indian households. They grow on poor soil, need very little water and can survive high temperatures, which makes them ideal for a country where more than half the farmland depends on rain. Nutritionally, they are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and they release sugar into the blood slowly, which helps in controlling diabetes. After the Green Revolution of the 1960s, however, government support went mainly to rice and wheat, and millets came to be seen as the 'poor man's food'. Their share in the Indian plate shrank steadily. In recent years the trend has begun to reverse. The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets on India's proposal, and many states now serve millet dishes in school meals. Nutrition experts welcome the change but warn that the revival will last only if farmers receive a fair price for what they grow.

According to the passage, why are millets well suited to India?

options.en: They give the highest yield of all cereals.
They grow on poor soil with very little water.
They are easy to export to other countries.

explanation_en: The passage says millets 'grow on poor soil, need very little water and can survive high temperatures', which suits a country where most farmland depends on rain.

options.en: Millets will soon replace rice and wheat completely.

question_en:
Passage: When Meena Devi was posted to a government school in a small hill village, the building had two rooms, a leaking roof and forty children who came only on days when there was no work in the fields. Instead of complaining, she began by visiting every home in the evening. She listened to parents, learnt the local dialect and explained, without lecturing, why reading mattered. She turned the school veranda into a library with old newspapers and picture books collected from friends in the city. Within two years attendance had nearly doubled, and the village panchayat, moved by her persistence, repaired the roof with its own funds. Meena Devi never claimed the credit. 'The children did the work,' she said when a journalist asked about her success. 'I only kept the door open.'

Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.en: The Teacher Who Kept the Door Open

explanation_en: The passage is about how Meena Devi transformed a village school, and it ends with her line 'I only kept the door open'. The other titles cover only a detail.

How did Meena Devi begin her effort to improve the school?

options.en: By punishing children who stayed away
By visiting families and listening to parents
By asking the panchayat for funds
By writing to newspapers in the city

explanation_en: 'She began by visiting every home in the evening. She listened to parents...'. The panchayat repaired the roof later, on its own, and she never wrote to newspapers.

Select the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'persistence' as used in the passage.
explanation_en: 'Persistence' means continuing firmly despite difficulty. Its opposite is 'irresolution' (lack of firmness, wavering). Perseverance, determination and endurance are near-synonyms.

What does Meena Devi most likely mean by 'I only kept the door open'?

She guarded the school building at night.
She never locked the classroom door.

question_en:
Passage: Discipline is the (1) ______ of success in every field. A student who (2) ______ a fixed timetable finds it easier to complete the syllabus well (3) ______ the examination. Discipline does not mean living (4) ______ fear of punishment; it means controlling one's own habits. Those who learn this early in life seldom (5) ______ their goals.

Select the most appropriate option to fill blank (1).
Relevant sentence: Discipline is the (1) ______ of success in every field.
explanation_en: Discipline is presented as the base on which success is built, so 'foundation' fits. 'Enemy' contradicts the passage and 'ceiling' and 'result' make no sense here.

question_en:
Passage: Discipline is the (1) ______ of success in every field. A student who (2) ______ a fixed timetable finds it easier to complete the syllabus well (3) ______ the examination. Discipline does not mean living (4) ______ fear of punishment; it means controlling one's own habits. Those who learn this early in life seldom (5) ______ their goals.

Select the most appropriate option to fill blank (2).
Relevant sentence: A student who (2) ______ a fixed timetable finds it easier to complete the syllabus...
explanation_en: Only a student who follows a timetable would find it easier to finish the syllabus; the other three verbs reverse the meaning.

question_en:
Passage: Discipline is the (1) ______ of success in every field. A student who (2) ______ a fixed timetable finds it easier to complete the syllabus well (3) ______ the examination. Discipline does not mean living (4) ______ fear of punishment; it means controlling one's own habits. Those who learn this early in life seldom (5) ______ their goals.

Select the most appropriate option to fill blank (3).
Relevant sentence: ...finds it easier to complete the syllabus well (3) ______ the examination.
explanation_en: 'Well before the examination' means comfortably ahead of it, which is the advantage of discipline. 'After' and 'during' are illogical and 'since' needs a past starting point.

question_en:
Passage: Discipline is the (1) ______ of success in every field. A student who (2) ______ a fixed timetable finds it easier to complete the syllabus well (3) ______ the examination. Discipline does not mean living (4) ______ fear of punishment; it means controlling one's own habits. Those who learn this early in life seldom (5) ______ their goals.

Select the most appropriate option to fill blank (4).
Relevant sentence: Discipline does not mean living (4) ______ fear of punishment.
explanation_en: The fixed phrase is 'live in fear of' something. 'Under', 'with' and 'from' do not combine with 'fear of' in this sense.

question_en:
Passage: Discipline is the (1) ______ of success in every field. A student who (2) ______ a fixed timetable finds it easier to complete the syllabus well (3) ______ the examination. Discipline does not mean living (4) ______ fear of punishment; it means controlling one's own habits. Those who learn this early in life seldom (5) ______ their goals.

Select the most appropriate option to fill blank (5).
Relevant sentence: Those who learn this early in life seldom (5) ______ their goals.
explanation_en: 'Seldom' is negative in meaning, so the verb must describe failure: disciplined people 'seldom miss their goals'. 'Seldom reach/achieve/set' would say the opposite of the passage.
